title: Alan Wake 2
summary: Diegetic, minimal UX for the case board, maps, inventory and photo mode of a narrative survival-horror game.

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Game and narrative design, UI and game programmers

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: Maps, menus, case board, dioramas, inventory, weapon quick-select, photo mode, lore browsers

sections.heading: Diegetic, minimal UI
body: I supported the game and narrative design teams and worked closely with UI and game programmers. The direction was diegetic and minimal: interfaces should feel like part of the game world.

sections.heading: Case board
body: The case board lets players physically arrange evidence to piece the plot together. It's an object in the game world, so no standard UI pattern applied.
sections.pull: Almost everything about the case board had to be found by hand, through iteration.

media.alt: Saga picks up a manuscript page in the general store
media.caption: New evidence found in the world, which then goes on the case board

sections.heading: Case board prototypes
body: Together with lead UI/UX designer we tried many setups and interactions, testing how players laid out, connected and read their evidence, until the board felt like a real space for thinking and following a narrative.

media.alt: Case board with a clue pinned to a question and Saga's thought beside it
media.caption: Case board. Built with the craft team and other teams on the project.

sections.heading: Dioramas
body: Dioramas are camera close-ups of spaces that hold clues and evidence. I worked out simple iconography, how players interact with the clues and a non-intrusive way to show text.
The UI had to stay a complementary layer to the player's fantasy of being an investigator who figures everything out.

Some dioramas have PCs the player can use to read emails, look through images or type in passwords that unlock new paths. The fictional UI looks like a 90s PC, but I designed the controls controller first, so it feels natural to use with a gamepad.

media.alt: Diorama close-up of a heart with a clue icon and a line of text
media.caption: Diorama

media.alt: In-game PC showing a 90s-style mail app
media.caption: PC mail

sections.heading: Maps
body: The same map has to work for a whole forest and a single house. I designed map navigation and camera controls, and worked through everything the map shows, from item pickups to mission markers.

sections.heading: Inventory
body: Items take up physical space in the inventory, and that one rule drove every interaction: drop bullets on a matching stack and they combine, place a different item and the grid rearranges itself.
I also designed the weapon quick-select, a customizable HUD element where players arrange weapons and tools however they like, and the lore browsers for text, audio and video.

media.alt: Lore browser showing a manuscript page
media.caption: Lore browser

sections.heading: Photo mode
body: The photo mode uses camera terms and values a photographer would recognize, plus tools only a game can offer, like an orbital camera that isn't tied to a physical lens position.
We built it for virtual photographers, and to get their shots of the game onto social media.

sections.heading: Awards
body: In 2024, Alan Wake 2 won Best Photo Mode at The Virtual Photography Awards and placed second for Photo Mode UX.
